To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The rate of production from 14C-glucose of 14CO(2) is decreased in the presence of unlabelled 14C-glutamine, 14C-ketone bodies and 14C-glucuronate in the brain homogenate of young and adult rat, and 2) The rate of 14C-keto body oxidation is enhanced by the addition of 14C-glutenate in the brain tissue of young rat.

in brain homogenate of young rats, 3-hydroxbutyrate and acetoacateate are oxidized by the same pathway, and the oxidation of glucose is decreased when either of the two ketone bodies is added, but in adult rats only 3-hydoxybutyrate is oxidized by this pathway, and its oxidation is decreased by the addition of glucose, but not of acetoacetate.

the rates of conversion into CO2 of D-3-hydroxy-[3-14C]-butyrate, acetoacetate, glucose, and glutamine were measured in presence or absence of unlabelleld alternative oxidizable substrata in whole homogenate from the brains of suckling and adult rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of metabolic pathways in developing and adult brain.
the role of the brain in the control of the blood ketone body levels.
the study of the metabolism of ketone bodies in rat brain and the interaction of these substrates with other metabolites.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain of the adult rat is able to use ketone bodies as an energy source, and is able to use glucose as an energy source in the presence of ketone bodies.
the brain of suckling animals is more dependent on glucose than that of adult animals, and that the ketone bodies are more readily oxidized in the adult.
the pattern of competition and cooperation among the various substrates was different in the brain of young rats than in adult rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the adult brain, glucose, ketone bodies and glutamine are oxidized independently of each other, whereas in young animals, the three substrates are in competition.
the brain is a very active organ in terms of its metabolic activity.

in young brain tissue there is an enhanced competition for oxidation of 14C-labelled glucose, ketone bodies and glutamine, but in adult tissue there is a competition between 3-hydroxylated compounds only, whereas the oxidation of 14-labelled glutamine and ketone bodies is not affected by unlabelled alternative substrates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the competition for oxidation among different substrates is a complex and dynamic process, and that the pattern of competition changes during development.
the brain of young animals is more dependent upon the oxidation of glutamine and ketone bodies, whereas that of adults depends upon glucose and ketone bodies.
the metabolic fate of glucose in brain tissue is not fixed, and can be influenced by other substrates present in the tissue, and that this is particularly so in the suckling rat.
